Training Dynamics

Cluster BB.4 · Training Dynamics

Exact learning dynamics of deep linear networks -- loss-landscape geometry, balanced gradient flow and the NTK, the rich (saddle-to-saddle) and lazy regimes, their mixed unification, and the implicit bias of SGD noise.

By Guillaume Corlouer (Stormglass)

  • PDFviewdownload
  • LaTeXdownload
  • Markdowndownload
  • SlidesviewdownloadLaTeX

\gdef\tightlist{\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}}

What you’ll learn

Motivation

  • Know about some big open questions in learning dynamics
  • Understand the concept of implicit regularization
  • Know about the different approaches to studying learning dynamics
  • Understand the AI safety motivations for learning dynamics
  • Know about emergent misalignment as a safety-relevant phenomena that illustrates the importance of understanding generalization for AI safety

Geometry and dynamics of deep neural networks

  • Know key results about the loss landscape of deep linear networks (DLNs): critical points are saddles or global minima
  • Explain the edge of stability phenomenon
  • Understand that gradient flow can be written as NTK-weighted gradient in function space
  • DLNs are degenerate and have conserved quantities through gradient flow

Regimes of learning in deep linear networks

  • Understand the role of initialization, width and depth for the lazy and rich (saddle to saddle) regimes in DLNs
  • Know about implicit regularization from non-linearity (neural race reduction)

References: (Saxe et al. 2014), (Achour et al. 2024), (Tu et al. 2024).

1. Setup and notation

We study deep linear networks (DLNs) with LLL weight matrices W1∈Rd1×d0,W2∈Rd2×d1,…,WL∈RdL×dL−1W_{1} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_0}, W_{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_2 \times d_1}, \ldots, W_{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_L \times d_{L-1}}W1​∈Rd1​×d0​,W2​∈Rd2​×d1​,…,WL​∈RdL​×dL−1​. The network computes:

f(x)=WLWL−1⋯W1 x=:Wxf(x) = W_{L} W_{L-1}\cdots W_{1} \, x =: W xf(x)=WL​WL−1​⋯W1​x=:Wx

where W=WL⋯W1∈RdL×d0W = W_{L} \cdots W_{1} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_L \times d_0}W=WL​⋯W1​∈RdL​×d0​ is the end-to-end (or "student") matrix. We train on a dataset {(xμ,yμ)}μ=1N\{(x_{\mu}, y_{\mu})\}_{\mu=1}^{N}{(xμ​,yμ​)}μ=1N​ with the squared loss:

L(θ)=12N∑μ=1N∥yμ−WL⋯W1 xμ∥2\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{2N}\sum_{\mu=1}^{N}\|y_{\mu} - W_{L} \cdots W_{1} \, x_{\mu}\|^{2}L(θ)=2N1​μ=1∑N​∥yμ​−WL​⋯W1​xμ​∥2

In the population limit with whitened inputs ΣX=I\Sigma_{X} = IΣX​=I, this becomes:

L(W)=12∥M−W∥F2\mathcal{L}(W) = \frac{1}{2}\|M - W\|_{F}^{2}L(W)=21​∥M−W∥F2​

where M=ΣYXΣX−1M = \Sigma_{YX}\Sigma_{X}^{-1}M=ΣYX​ΣX−1​ is the "teacher" matrix (the OLS solution) with SVD M=U diag(s1,…,sr,0,…,0) V⊤M = U \,\text{diag}(s_{1}, \ldots, s_{r}, 0, \ldots, 0)\, V^{\top}M=Udiag(s1​,…,sr​,0,…,0)V⊤, and s1≥s2≥⋯≥sr>0s_{1} \geq s_{2} \geq \cdots \geq s_{r} > 0s1​≥s2​≥⋯≥sr​>0.

2. Loss landscape geometry

This problem explores the critical point structure of deep linear networks, following (Achour et al. 2024).

Exercise 2.1 (Diagonal decomposition). Consider the diagonal case: d0=d1=⋯=dL=dd_{0} = d_{1} = \cdots = d_{L} = dd0​=d1​=⋯=dL​=d, and the teacher is diagonal, M=diag(s1,…,sd)M = \text{diag}(s_{1}, \ldots, s_{d})M=diag(s1​,…,sd​), with s1>s2>⋯>sd>0s_{1} > s_{2} > \cdots > s_{d} > 0s1​>s2​>⋯>sd​>0. Restrict attention to diagonal weight matrices Wl=diag(wl(1),…,wl(d))W_{l} = \text{diag}(w_{l}^{(1)}, \ldots, w_{l}^{(d)})Wl​=diag(wl(1)​,…,wl(d)​). Show that the loss decomposes into ddd independent scalar problems:

L=12∑α=1d(sα−∏l=1Lwl(α))2\mathcal{L}= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{d} \left(s_{\alpha} - \prod_{l=1}^{L} w_{l}^{(\alpha)}\right)^{2}L=21​α=1∑d​(sα​−l=1∏L​wl(α)​)2
Solution

When all WlW_{l}Wl​ are diagonal, the product W=WL⋯W1W = W_{L} \cdots W_{1}W=WL​⋯W1​ is also diagonal with entries (W)αα=∏l=1Lwl(α)(W)_{\alpha\alpha}= \prod_{l=1}^{L} w_{l}^{(\alpha)}(W)αα​=∏l=1L​wl(α)​. The teacher MMM is diagonal with entries sαs_{\alpha}sα​. Then:

L=12∥M−W∥F2=12∑α=1d(sα−(W)αα)2=12∑α=1d(sα−∏l=1Lwl(α))2\mathcal{L}= \frac{1}{2}\|M - W\|_{F}^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{d} (s_{\alpha} - (W)_{\alpha\alpha})^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{d} \left(s_{\alpha} - \prod_{l=1}^{L} w_{l}^{(\alpha)}\right)^{2}L=21​∥M−W∥F2​=21​α=1∑d​(sα​−(W)αα​)2=21​α=1∑d​(sα​−l=1∏L​wl(α)​)2

Since the different modes α\alphaα share no parameters, the loss decomposes into ddd independent scalar problems. □\square□

Exercise 2.2 (Scalar critical points). For a single scalar mode with target s>0s > 0s>0, find all first-order critical points of ℓ(w1,w2)=12(s−w1w2)2\ell(w_{1}, w_{2}) = \frac{1}{2}(s - w_{1} w_{2})^{2}ℓ(w1​,w2​)=21​(s−w1​w2​)2 at depth L=2L = 2L=2. Show that the critical points are:

  • The global minimum manifold: w1w2=sw_{1} w_{2} = sw1​w2​=s
  • The origin: w1=w2=0w_{1} = w_{2} = 0w1​=w2​=0

Classify the origin as a saddle point by computing the Hessian HHH of ℓ\ellℓ at (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) and showing it has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Hint: Write the gradient equations

Solution

For L=2L = 2L=2, the gradient equations are:

∂ℓ∂w1=−(s−w1w2) w2=0,∂ℓ∂w2=−(s−w1w2) w1=0\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial w_{1}}= -(s - w_{1} w_{2})\,w_{2} = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial w_{2}}= -(s - w_{1} w_{2})\,w_{1} = 0∂w1​∂ℓ​=−(s−w1​w2​)w2​=0,∂w2​∂ℓ​=−(s−w1​w2​)w1​=0

Case 1: s−w1w2=0s - w_{1} w_{2} = 0s−w1​w2​=0, i.e. w1w2=sw_{1} w_{2} = sw1​w2​=s. This is the global minimum manifold (a hyperbola w2=s/w1w_{2} = s/w_{1}w2​=s/w1​) with ℓ=0\ell = 0ℓ=0.

Case 2: If s−w1w2≠0s - w_{1} w_{2} \neq 0s−w1​w2​=0, then the first equation requires w2=0w_{2} = 0w2​=0 and the second requires w1=0w_{1} = 0w1​=0. (For instance, if w2≠0w_{2} \neq 0w2​=0 and w1=0w_{1} = 0w1​=0, the first equation gives −s w2=0-s\,w_{2} = 0−sw2​=0, which contradicts s>0s > 0s>0 and w2≠0w_{2} \neq 0w2​=0.) So the only other critical point is w1=w2=0w_{1} = w_{2} = 0w1​=w2​=0.

The Hessian at (0,0)(0,0)(0,0). We need the second derivatives of ℓ=12(s−w1w2)2\ell = \frac{1}{2}(s - w_{1} w_{2})^{2}ℓ=21​(s−w1​w2​)2:

∂2ℓ∂w12=w22,∂2ℓ∂w22=w12,∂2ℓ∂w1∂w2=−(s−w1w2)+w1w2=2w1w2−s\frac{\partial^{2} \ell}{\partial w_{1}^{2}}= w_{2}^{2}, \qquad \frac{\partial^{2} \ell}{\partial w_{2}^{2}}= w_{1}^{2}, \qquad \frac{\partial^{2} \ell}{\partial w_{1} \partial w_{2}}= -(s - w_{1} w_{2}) + w_{1} w_{2} = 2w_{1} w_{2} - s∂w12​∂2ℓ​=w22​,∂w22​∂2ℓ​=w12​,∂w1​∂w2​∂2ℓ​=−(s−w1​w2​)+w1​w2​=2w1​w2​−s

At (0,0)(0,0)(0,0):

H=(0−s−s0)H = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -s \\ -s & 0\end{pmatrix}H=(0−s​−s0​)

The eigenvalues are ±s\pm s±s. Since s>0s > 0s>0, HHH has one positive and one negative eigenvalue. The origin is a strict saddle point. □\square□

Exercise 2.3 (Critical-point structure). Achour et al. (Achour et al. 2024) show that every first-order critical point θ=(W1,…,WL)\theta = (W_{1}, \ldots, W_{L})θ=(W1​,…,WL​) satisfies: there exists a subset S⊆{1,…,d}S \subseteq \{1, \ldots, d\}S⊆{1,…,d} such that

W=WL⋯W1=PS MW = W_{L} \cdots W_{1} = P_{S}\, MW=WL​⋯W1​=PS​M

where PS=USUS⊤P_{S} = U_{S} U_{S}^{\top}PS​=US​US⊤​ is the orthogonal projector onto the span of the left singular vectors {uα}α∈S\{u_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha \in S}{uα​}α∈S​ of MMM. For the diagonal case M=diag(s1,…,sd)M = \text{diag}(s_{1}, \ldots, s_{d})M=diag(s1​,…,sd​), write the value of the loss at the critical point corresponding to S={1,…,r}S = \{1, \ldots, r\}S={1,…,r} with r<dr < dr<d.

Solution

At the critical point W=PSMW = P_{S} MW=PS​M with S={1,…,r}S = \{1, \ldots, r\}S={1,…,r}, the student retains only the first rrr modes: W=diag(s1,…,sr,0,…,0)W = \text{diag}(s_{1}, \ldots, s_{r}, 0, \ldots, 0)W=diag(s1​,…,sr​,0,…,0). The loss is:

L=12∥M−PSM∥F2=12∑α∉Ssα2=12∑α=r+1dsα2\mathcal{L}= \frac{1}{2}\|M - P_{S} M\|_{F}^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha \notin S}s_{\alpha}^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha=r+1}^{d} s_{\alpha}^{2}L=21​∥M−PS​M∥F2​=21​α∈/S∑​sα2​=21​α=r+1∑d​sα2​

This is strictly positive whenever r<dr < dr<d (since all sα>0s_{\alpha} > 0sα​>0), so these are not global minima. By the Hessian analysis (extending Exercise 2.2), the direction corresponding to "switching on" a missing mode α∉S\alpha \notin Sα∈/S is a descent direction, making these critical points saddle points. All critical points with ∣S∣=d|S| = d∣S∣=d have W=MW = MW=M and L=0\mathcal{L}= 0L=0: these are the global minima. Therefore there are no spurious local minima — every local minimum is global. □\square□

Exercise 2.4 (Symmetry of the global minima). The group GLh:=GLd1×⋯×GLdL−1GL_{h} := GL_{d_1}\times \cdots \times GL_{d_{L-1}}GLh​:=GLd1​​×⋯×GLdL−1​​ acts on the weights by:

(W1,…,WL)↦(g1W1,  g2W2g1−1,  …,  WLgL−1−1)(W_{1}, \ldots, W_{L}) \mapsto (g_{1} W_{1},\; g_{2} W_{2} g_{1}^{-1},\; \ldots,\; W_{L} g_{L-1}^{-1})(W1​,…,WL​)↦(g1​W1​,g2​W2​g1−1​,…,WL​gL−1−1​)

Verify that the student map μ(θ)=WL⋯W1\mu(\theta) = W_{L} \cdots W_{1}μ(θ)=WL​⋯W1​ is invariant under this action: μ(g⋅θ)=μ(θ)\mu(g \cdot \theta) = \mu(\theta)μ(g⋅θ)=μ(θ). What does this imply about the dimension of the set of global minima in parameter space?

Solution

Under the group action:

μ(g⋅θ)=WLgL−1−1⋅gL−1WL−1gL−2−1⋅…⋅g1W1=WLWL−1⋯W1=μ(θ)\mu(g \cdot \theta) = W_{L} g_{L-1}^{-1}\cdot g_{L-1}W_{L-1}g_{L-2}^{-1}\cdot \ldots \cdot g_{1} W_{1} = W_{L} W_{L-1}\cdots W_{1} = \mu(\theta)μ(g⋅θ)=WL​gL−1−1​⋅gL−1​WL−1​gL−2−1​⋅…⋅g1​W1​=WL​WL−1​⋯W1​=μ(θ)

All glg_{l}gl​ and gl−1g_{l}^{-1}gl−1​ factors cancel telescopically. This means every parameter point in the orbit Oθ=GLh⋅θ\mathcal{O}_{\theta} = GL_{h} \cdot \thetaOθ​=GLh​⋅θ maps to the same student WWW. The global minima form the fiber μ−1(M)\mu^{-1}(M)μ−1(M), which contains the entire orbit GLh⋅θ∗GL_{h} \cdot \theta^{*}GLh​⋅θ∗ for any global minimizer θ∗\theta^{*}θ∗. The orbit has dimension ∑l=1L−1dl2\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}d_{l}^{2}∑l=1L−1​dl2​ (the dimension of GLhGL_{h}GLh​), so the set of global minima is a continuous manifold of very high dimension — far from being isolated points. □\square□

3. Gradient flow and conserved quantities

We now study gradient flow: θ˙(t)=−∇θL(θ(t))\dot{\theta}(t) = -\nabla_{\theta} \mathcal{L}(\theta(t))θ˙(t)=−∇θ​L(θ(t)), the continuous-time limit of gradient descent with infinitesimal learning rate.

Exercise 3.1 (Gradient-flow equations). For a two-layer diagonal DLN (L=2L=2L=2) with loss L=12∥M−W2W1∥F2\mathcal{L}= \frac{1}{2}\|M - W_{2} W_{1}\|_{F}^{2}L=21​∥M−W2​W1​∥F2​, assume that each weight matrix WiW_{i}Wi​ is a diagonal matrix and whitened inputs. Derive the gradient flow equations for each layer. Show that:

W˙1=W2⊤(M−W2W1),W˙2=(M−W2W1)W1⊤\dot{W}_{1} = W_{2}^{\top}(M - W_{2} W_{1}), \qquad \dot{W}_{2} = (M - W_{2} W_{1}) W_{1}^{\top}W˙1​=W2⊤​(M−W2​W1​),W˙2​=(M−W2​W1​)W1⊤​
Solution

We have L=12∥M−W2W1∥F2=12Tr[(M−W2W1)⊤(M−W2W1)]\mathcal{L}= \frac{1}{2}\|M - W_{2} W_{1}\|_{F}^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\text{Tr}\left[(M - W_{2} W_{1})^{\top}(M - W_{2} W_{1})\right]L=21​∥M−W2​W1​∥F2​=21​Tr[(M−W2​W1​)⊤(M−W2​W1​)].

General matrix derivation. Expand:

L=12Tr(M⊤M)−Tr(M⊤W2W1)+12Tr(W1⊤W2⊤W2W1)\mathcal{L}= \frac{1}{2}\text{Tr}(M^{\top} M) - \text{Tr}(M^{\top} W_{2} W_{1}) + \frac{1}{2}\text{Tr}(W_{1}^{\top} W_{2}^{\top} W_{2} W_{1})L=21​Tr(M⊤M)−Tr(M⊤W2​W1​)+21​Tr(W1⊤​W2⊤​W2​W1​)

Differentiating with respect to W1W_{1}W1​, using ∂∂ATr(B⊤A)=B\frac{\partial}{\partial A}\text{Tr}(B^{\top} A) = B∂A∂​Tr(B⊤A)=B and ∂∂ATr(A⊤CA)=(C+C⊤)A\frac{\partial}{\partial A}\text{Tr}(A^{\top} C A) = (C + C^{\top})A∂A∂​Tr(A⊤CA)=(C+C⊤)A:

∇W1L=−W2⊤M+W2⊤W2W1=−W2⊤(M−W2W1)\nabla_{W_1}\mathcal{L}= -W_{2}^{\top} M + W_{2}^{\top} W_{2} W_{1} = -W_{2}^{\top}(M - W_{2} W_{1})∇W1​​L=−W2⊤​M+W2⊤​W2​W1​=−W2⊤​(M−W2​W1​)

So W˙1=−∇W1L=W2⊤(M−W2W1)\dot{W}_{1} = -\nabla_{W_1}\mathcal{L}= W_{2}^{\top}(M - W_{2} W_{1})W˙1​=−∇W1​​L=W2⊤​(M−W2​W1​).

Similarly, ∇W2L=−(M−W2W1)W1⊤\nabla_{W_2}\mathcal{L}= -(M - W_{2} W_{1})W_{1}^{\top}∇W2​​L=−(M−W2​W1​)W1⊤​, giving W˙2=(M−W2W1)W1⊤\dot{W}_{2} = (M - W_{2} W_{1})W_{1}^{\top}W˙2​=(M−W2​W1​)W1⊤​.

Diagonal shortcut. For diagonal matrices W1=diag(aα)W_{1} = \text{diag}(a_{\alpha})W1​=diag(aα​), W2=diag(bα)W_{2} = \text{diag}(b_{\alpha})W2​=diag(bα​), M=diag(sα)M = \text{diag}(s_{\alpha})M=diag(sα​): the loss decouples as L=12∑α(sα−bαaα)2\mathcal{L}= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha} - b_{\alpha} a_{\alpha})^{2}L=21​∑α​(sα​−bα​aα​)2. Then a˙α=−∂L/∂aα=bα(sα−bαaα)\dot{a}_{\alpha} = -\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial a_{\alpha} = b_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha} - b_{\alpha} a_{\alpha})a˙α​=−∂L/∂aα​=bα​(sα​−bα​aα​) and b˙α=aα(sα−bαaα)\dot{b}_{\alpha} = a_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha} - b_{\alpha} a_{\alpha})b˙α​=aα​(sα​−bα​aα​), which is the diagonal version of the matrix equations above. □\square□

Exercise 3.2 (Balancedness is conserved). Define the balancedness matrix:

G:=W2⊤W2−W1W1⊤G := W_{2}^{\top} W_{2} - W_{1} W_{1}^{\top}G:=W2⊤​W2​−W1​W1⊤​

Show that GGG is conserved under the gradient flow, i.e. G˙=0\dot{G}= 0G˙=0. In other words, gradient flow is constrained on the balanced manifold

Mβ:={θ∈Ω∣Wℓ+1⊤Wℓ+1−WℓWℓ⊤=βℓ,  ℓ=1,…,L−1}.\mathcal{M}_{\beta}:= \{\theta\in\Omega\mid W_{\ell+1}^{\top}W_{\ell+1}- W_{\ell}W_{\ell}^{\top}= \beta_{\ell},\; \ell=1,\ldots,L-1\}.Mβ​:={θ∈Ω∣Wℓ+1⊤​Wℓ+1​−Wℓ​Wℓ⊤​=βℓ​,ℓ=1,…,L−1}.

Hint: Compute G˙\dot{G}G˙, substitute the gradient flow equations and verify that the terms cancel pairwise.

Solution

Let E:=M−W2W1E := M - W_{2} W_{1}E:=M−W2​W1​ denote the residual. Compute:

G˙=W˙2⊤W2+W2⊤W˙2−W˙1W1⊤−W1W˙1⊤\dot{G}= \dot{W}_{2}^{\top} W_{2} + W_{2}^{\top} \dot{W}_{2} - \dot{W}_{1} W_{1}^{\top} - W_{1} \dot{W}_{1}^{\top}G˙=W˙2⊤​W2​+W2⊤​W˙2​−W˙1​W1⊤​−W1​W˙1⊤​

Substitute the gradient flow equations. Using W˙2=EW1⊤\dot{W}_{2} = E W_{1}^{\top}W˙2​=EW1⊤​ and W˙1=W2⊤E\dot{W}_{1} = W_{2}^{\top} EW˙1​=W2⊤​E:

W˙2⊤W2=(EW1⊤)⊤W2=W1E⊤W2\dot{W}_{2}^{\top} W_{2} = (E W_{1}^{\top})^{\top} W_{2} = W_{1} E^{\top} W_{2}W˙2⊤​W2​=(EW1⊤​)⊤W2​=W1​E⊤W2​W2⊤W˙2=W2⊤EW1⊤W_{2}^{\top} \dot{W}_{2} = W_{2}^{\top} E W_{1}^{\top}W2⊤​W˙2​=W2⊤​EW1⊤​W˙1W1⊤=W2⊤EW1⊤\dot{W}_{1} W_{1}^{\top} = W_{2}^{\top} E W_{1}^{\top}W˙1​W1⊤​=W2⊤​EW1⊤​W1W˙1⊤=W1(W2⊤E)⊤=W1E⊤W2W_{1} \dot{W}_{1}^{\top} = W_{1}(W_{2}^{\top} E)^{\top} = W_{1} E^{\top} W_{2}W1​W˙1⊤​=W1​(W2⊤​E)⊤=W1​E⊤W2​

Therefore:

G˙=W1E⊤W2+W2⊤EW1⊤−W2⊤EW1⊤−W1E⊤W2=0\dot{G}= W_{1} E^{\top} W_{2} + W_{2}^{\top} E W_{1}^{\top} - W_{2}^{\top} E W_{1}^{\top} - W_{1} E^{\top} W_{2} = 0G˙=W1​E⊤W2​+W2⊤​EW1⊤​−W2⊤​EW1⊤​−W1​E⊤W2​=0

The terms cancel pairwise. GGG is conserved. □\square□

From now on, assume balanced initialization: G(0)=0G(0) = 0G(0)=0, which by Exercise 3.2 means W2⊤W2=W1W1⊤W_{2}^{\top} W_{2} = W_{1} W_{1}^{\top}W2⊤​W2​=W1​W1⊤​ for all time. We want to derive the gradient flow in function space (the ODE for the student W=W2W1W = W_{2} W_{1}W=W2​W1​). This requires several steps.

Exercise 3.3 (Function-space velocity). Compute W˙:=ddt(W2W1)\dot{W}:= \frac{d}{dt}(W_{2} W_{1})W˙:=dtd​(W2​W1​) using the gradient flow equations from Exercise 3.1. Show that:

W˙=(M−W) W1⊤W1+W2W2⊤ (M−W)\dot{W}= (M - W)\, W_{1}^{\top} W_{1} + W_{2} W_{2}^{\top}\, (M - W)W˙=(M−W)W1⊤​W1​+W2​W2⊤​(M−W)
Solution

Apply the product rule:

W˙=W˙2W1+W2W˙1=(M−W2W1)W1⊤⋅W1+W2⋅W2⊤(M−W2W1)\dot{W}= \dot{W}_{2} W_{1} + W_{2} \dot{W}_{1} = (M - W_{2} W_{1})W_{1}^{\top} \cdot W_{1} + W_{2} \cdot W_{2}^{\top}(M - W_{2} W_{1})W˙=W˙2​W1​+W2​W˙1​=(M−W2​W1​)W1⊤​⋅W1​+W2​⋅W2⊤​(M−W2​W1​)

Writing W=W2W1W = W_{2} W_{1}W=W2​W1​:

W˙=(M−W) W1⊤W1+W2W2⊤ (M−W)□\dot{W}= (M - W)\,W_{1}^{\top} W_{1} + W_{2} W_{2}^{\top}\,(M - W) \qquad \squareW˙=(M−W)W1⊤​W1​+W2​W2⊤​(M−W)□

Exercise 3.4 (W1⊤W1W_{1}^{\top}W_{1}W1⊤​W1​ in terms of WWW). We now need to express W1⊤W1W_{1}^{\top} W_{1}W1⊤​W1​ and W2W2⊤W_{2} W_{2}^{\top}W2​W2⊤​ in terms of W=W2W1W = W_{2} W_{1}W=W2​W1​. For simplicity, assume that the weight matrices WlW_{l}Wl​ are diagonal. Show that:

W1⊤W1=(W⊤W)1/2W_{1}^{\top} W_{1} = (W^{\top} W)^{1/2}W1⊤​W1​=(W⊤W)1/2
Solution

For diagonal matrices, W1=diag(aα)W_{1} = \text{diag}(a_{\alpha})W1​=diag(aα​) and W2=diag(bα)W_{2} = \text{diag}(b_{\alpha})W2​=diag(bα​) with W=diag(aαbα)W = \text{diag}(a_{\alpha} b_{\alpha})W=diag(aα​bα​). Balancedness gives bα2=aα2b_{\alpha}^{2} = a_{\alpha}^{2}bα2​=aα2​ for each α\alphaα, i.e. ∣bα∣=∣aα∣|b_{\alpha}| = |a_{\alpha}|∣bα​∣=∣aα​∣ (with matching signs for positive entries).

Now W1⊤W1=diag(aα2)W_{1}^{\top} W_{1} = \text{diag}(a_{\alpha}^{2})W1⊤​W1​=diag(aα2​) and W⊤W=diag(aα2bα2)W^{\top} W = \text{diag}(a_{\alpha}^{2} b_{\alpha}^{2})W⊤W=diag(aα2​bα2​). Using bα2=aα2b_{\alpha}^{2} = a_{\alpha}^{2}bα2​=aα2​:

W⊤W=diag(aα2⋅aα2)=diag(aα4)W^{\top} W = \text{diag}(a_{\alpha}^{2} \cdot a_{\alpha}^{2}) = \text{diag}(a_{\alpha}^{4})W⊤W=diag(aα2​⋅aα2​)=diag(aα4​)

Taking the positive square root:

(W⊤W)1/2=diag(aα2)=W1⊤W1□(W^{\top} W)^{1/2}= \text{diag}(a_{\alpha}^{2}) = W_{1}^{\top} W_{1} \qquad \square(W⊤W)1/2=diag(aα2​)=W1⊤​W1​□

Exercise 3.5 (W2W2⊤W_{2}W_{2}^{\top}W2​W2⊤​ in terms of WWW). Similarly, show that W2W2⊤=(WW⊤)1/2W_{2} W_{2}^{\top} = (W W^{\top})^{1/2}W2​W2⊤​=(WW⊤)1/2.

Solution

By the same argument, W2W2⊤=diag(bα2)=diag(aα2)W_{2} W_{2}^{\top} = \text{diag}(b_{\alpha}^{2}) = \text{diag}(a_{\alpha}^{2})W2​W2⊤​=diag(bα2​)=diag(aα2​) (using bα2=aα2b_{\alpha}^{2} = a_{\alpha}^{2}bα2​=aα2​). And WW⊤=diag(aα2bα2)=diag(aα4)WW^{\top} = \text{diag}(a_{\alpha}^{2} b_{\alpha}^{2}) = \text{diag}(a_{\alpha}^{4})WW⊤=diag(aα2​bα2​)=diag(aα4​), so (WW⊤)1/2=diag(aα2)=W2W2⊤(WW^{\top})^{1/2}= \text{diag}(a_{\alpha}^{2}) = W_{2} W_{2}^{\top}(WW⊤)1/2=diag(aα2​)=W2​W2⊤​. □\square□

Exercise 3.6 (The balanced function-space ODE). Substitute the results of Exercise 3.4 and 3.5 into Exercise 3.3 to obtain:

W˙=(WW⊤)1/2(M−W)+(M−W)(W⊤W)1/2\dot{W}= (W W^{\top})^{1/2}(M - W) + (M - W)(W^{\top} W)^{1/2}W˙=(WW⊤)1/2(M−W)+(M−W)(W⊤W)1/2
Solution

Substituting into Exercise 3.3:

W˙=(M−W)(W⊤W)1/2+(WW⊤)1/2(M−W)□\dot{W}= (M - W)(W^{\top} W)^{1/2}+ (WW^{\top})^{1/2}(M - W) \qquad \squareW˙=(M−W)(W⊤W)1/2+(WW⊤)1/2(M−W)□

Exercise 3.7 (The NTK operator). Define the NTK operator for L=2L = 2L=2 as:

K[F]:=(WW⊤)1/2 F+F (W⊤W)1/2K[F] := (WW^{\top})^{1/2}\, F + F\, (W^{\top} W)^{1/2}K[F]:=(WW⊤)1/2F+F(W⊤W)1/2

Show that the gradient flow from Exercise 3.6 can be written as W˙=K[M−W]\dot{W}= K[M - W]W˙=K[M−W].

It turns out that this result generalizes to depth LLL on the balanced manifold and to non-diagonal weight matrices:

W˙=∑k=1L(WW⊤)L−kL(M−W)(W⊤W)k−1L\dot{W}= \sum_{k=1}^{L}(WW^{\top})^{\frac{L-k}{L}}(M - W) (W^{\top} W)^{\frac{k-1}{L}}W˙=k=1∑L​(WW⊤)LL−k​(M−W)(W⊤W)Lk−1​

This is the NTK equation in the case of DLNs. The NTK equation is a gradient flow in function space with NTK being a preconditioning operator for the gradient.

Solution

With F=M−WF = M - WF=M−W, the equation from Exercise 3.6 reads:

W˙=(WW⊤)1/2 F+F (W⊤W)1/2=K[F]=K[M−W]□\dot{W}= (WW^{\top})^{1/2}\,F + F\,(W^{\top} W)^{1/2}= K[F] = K[M - W] \qquad \squareW˙=(WW⊤)1/2F+F(W⊤W)1/2=K[F]=K[M−W]□

The general depth-LLL result W˙=∑k=1L(WW⊤)(L−k)/L(M−W)(W⊤W)(k−1)/L\dot{W}= \sum_{k=1}^{L}(WW^{\top})^{(L-k)/L}(M-W)(W^{\top} W)^{(k-1)/L}W˙=∑k=1L​(WW⊤)(L−k)/L(M−W)(W⊤W)(k−1)/L follows from the same approach applied to the LLL-fold balanced conditions Wl+1⊤Wl+1=WlWl⊤W_{l+1}^{\top} W_{l+1}= W_{l} W_{l}^{\top}Wl+1⊤​Wl+1​=Wl​Wl⊤​ for all lll, and extends to non-diagonal matrices via the polar decomposition.

4. Rich regime: saddle-to-saddle

This is the core problem. We derive the exact solution of the rich regime dynamics directly from the self-consistent equation of Section 3, emphasizing the NTK perspective.

Alignment assumption. Start from the balanced gradient flow equation derived in Exercise 3.6:

W˙=(WW⊤)1/2(M−W)+(M−W)(W⊤W)1/2\dot{W}= (WW^{\top})^{1/2}(M - W) + (M - W)(W^{\top} W)^{1/2}W˙=(WW⊤)1/2(M−W)+(M−W)(W⊤W)1/2

We work in the rich regime (small initialization) with balanced weights. Assume that the student is aligned to the teacher: the singular vectors of W(t)W(t)W(t) coincide with those of MMM at all times. Concretely, write:

M=U diag(s1,…,sd) V⊤,W(t)=U diag(w1(t),…,wd(t)) V⊤M = U\,\text{diag}(s_{1}, \ldots, s_{d})\,V^{\top}, \qquad W(t) = U\,\text{diag}(w_{1}(t), \ldots, w_{d}(t))\,V^{\top}M=Udiag(s1​,…,sd​)V⊤,W(t)=Udiag(w1​(t),…,wd​(t))V⊤

where U,VU, VU,V are the left/right singular vectors of MMM, and wα(t)≥0w_{\alpha}(t) \geq 0wα​(t)≥0 are the evolving singular values of WWW.

Exercise 4.1 (Aligned NTK). Under this alignment assumption, show that the NTK operator is aligned to the task, i.e. K[F]K[F]K[F] preserves the SVD basis. In particular, show that:

(WW⊤)1/2=U diag(w1,…,wd) U⊤,(W⊤W)1/2=V diag(w1,…,wd) V⊤(WW^{\top})^{1/2}= U\,\text{diag}(w_{1}, \ldots, w_{d})\,U^{\top}, \qquad (W^{\top} W)^{1/2}= V\,\text{diag}(w_{1}, \ldots, w_{d})\,V^{\top}(WW⊤)1/2=Udiag(w1​,…,wd​)U⊤,(W⊤W)1/2=Vdiag(w1​,…,wd​)V⊤

and that the residual is M−W=U diag(s1−w1,…,sd−wd) V⊤M - W = U\,\text{diag}(s_{1} - w_{1}, \ldots, s_{d} - w_{d})\,V^{\top}M−W=Udiag(s1​−w1​,…,sd​−wd​)V⊤.

Hint: Recall that for A=U diag(σi) V⊤A = U\,\text{diag}(\sigma_{i})\,V^{\top}A=Udiag(σi​)V⊤, we have AA⊤=U diag(σi2) U⊤AA^{\top} = U\,\text{diag}(\sigma_{i}^{2})\,U^{\top}AA⊤=Udiag(σi2​)U⊤, and therefore (AA⊤)1/2=U diag(∣σi∣) U⊤(AA^{\top})^{1/2}= U\,\text{diag}(|\sigma_{i}|)\,U^{\top}(AA⊤)1/2=Udiag(∣σi​∣)U⊤.

Solution

Under the alignment assumption, W=U diag(wα) V⊤W = U\,\text{diag}(w_{\alpha})\,V^{\top}W=Udiag(wα​)V⊤. Then:

WW⊤=U diag(wα2) U⊤WW^{\top} = U\,\text{diag}(w_{\alpha}^{2})\,U^{\top}WW⊤=Udiag(wα2​)U⊤

Since wα≥0w_{\alpha} \geq 0wα​≥0, the positive matrix square root is:

(WW⊤)1/2=U diag(wα) U⊤(WW^{\top})^{1/2}= U\,\text{diag}(w_{\alpha})\,U^{\top}(WW⊤)1/2=Udiag(wα​)U⊤

Similarly:

W⊤W=V diag(wα2) V⊤⟹(W⊤W)1/2=V diag(wα) V⊤W^{\top} W = V\,\text{diag}(w_{\alpha}^{2})\,V^{\top} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad (W^{\top} W)^{1/2}= V\,\text{diag}(w_{\alpha})\,V^{\top}W⊤W=Vdiag(wα2​)V⊤⟹(W⊤W)1/2=Vdiag(wα​)V⊤

The residual is immediate:

M−W=U diag(sα−wα) V⊤M - W = U\,\text{diag}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})\,V^{\top}M−W=Udiag(sα​−wα​)V⊤

The NTK operator acts on any matrix F=U diag(fα) V⊤F = U\,\text{diag}(f_{\alpha})\,V^{\top}F=Udiag(fα​)V⊤ as:

K[F]=U diag(wα) U⊤U diag(fα) V⊤+U diag(fα) V⊤V diag(wα) V⊤=U diag(2wαfα) V⊤.\begin{aligned}K[F]&= U\,\text{diag}(w_{\alpha})\,U^{\top} U\,\text{diag}(f_{\alpha})\,V^{\top} \\&\quad + U\,\text{diag}(f_{\alpha})\,V^{\top} V\,\text{diag}(w_{\alpha})\,V^{\top} \\&= U\,\text{diag}(2w_{\alpha} f_{\alpha})\,V^{\top}.\end{aligned}K[F]​=Udiag(wα​)U⊤Udiag(fα​)V⊤+Udiag(fα​)V⊤Vdiag(wα​)V⊤=Udiag(2wα​fα​)V⊤.​

So K[F]K[F]K[F] stays in the SVD basis of MMM — the NTK is aligned to the task. □\square□

Exercise 4.2 (Decoupled scalar ODEs). Substitute into the self-consistent equation. Show that the matrix equation decouples into ddd independent scalar ODEs:

w˙α=2 wα (sα−wα),α=1,…,d\dot{w}_{\alpha} = 2\,w_{\alpha}\,(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha}), \qquad \alpha = 1, \ldots, dw˙α​=2wα​(sα​−wα​),α=1,…,d

Hint: Compute the product (WW⊤)1/2(M−W)(WW^{\top})^{1/2}(M - W)(WW⊤)1/2(M−W) in the SVD basis. It is diagonal with entries wα(sα−wα)w_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})wα​(sα​−wα​). The second term contributes identically, giving the factor of 2.

Solution

Substitute into W˙=(WW⊤)1/2(M−W)+(M−W)(W⊤W)1/2\dot{W}= (WW^{\top})^{1/2}(M-W) + (M-W)(W^{\top} W)^{1/2}W˙=(WW⊤)1/2(M−W)+(M−W)(W⊤W)1/2:

First term:

U diag(wα) U⊤U⏟I diag(sα−wα) V⊤=U diag(wα(sα−wα)) V⊤U\,\text{diag}(w_{\alpha})\,\underbrace{U^\top U}_{I}\,\text{diag}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})\,V^{\top} = U\,\text{diag}\big(w_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})\big)\,V^{\top}Udiag(wα​)IU⊤U​​diag(sα​−wα​)V⊤=Udiag(wα​(sα​−wα​))V⊤

Second term:

U diag(sα−wα) V⊤V⏟I diag(wα) V⊤=U diag((sα−wα) wα) V⊤U\,\text{diag}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})\,\underbrace{V^\top V}_{I}\,\text{diag}(w_{\alpha})\,V^{\top} = U\,\text{diag}\big((s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})\,w_{\alpha}\big)\,V^{\top}Udiag(sα​−wα​)IV⊤V​​diag(wα​)V⊤=Udiag((sα​−wα​)wα​)V⊤

Summing:

W˙=U diag(2 wα(sα−wα)) V⊤\dot{W}= U\,\text{diag}\big(2\,w_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})\big)\,V^{\top}W˙=Udiag(2wα​(sα​−wα​))V⊤

Since W=U diag(wα) V⊤W = U\,\text{diag}(w_{\alpha})\,V^{\top}W=Udiag(wα​)V⊤ and the singular vectors are constant by assumption, we read off:

w˙α=2 wα (sα−wα)\boxed{\dot{w}_\alpha = 2\,w_\alpha\,(s_\alpha - w_\alpha)}w˙α​=2wα​(sα​−wα​)​

The NTK perspective makes the structure transparent: the factor 2wα2w_{\alpha}2wα​ is the NTK eigenvalue for mode α\alphaα, which amplifies learning in directions that are already strong, while (sα−wα)(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})(sα​−wα​) is the residual. □\square□

Exercise 4.3 (Timescale of learning). The ODE w˙=2w(s−w)\dot{w}= 2w(s - w)w˙=2w(s−w) is a logistic equation whose solution is:

w(t)=s1+(sw0−1)e−2stw(t) = \frac{s}{1 + \left(\frac{s}{w_0}- 1\right)e^{-2st}}w(t)=1+(w0​s​−1)e−2sts​

where w0=w(0)w_{0} = w(0)w0​=w(0). Compute the time tαt_{\alpha}tα​ it takes for mode α\alphaα to travel from initial strength w0w_{0}w0​ to a final strength wfw_{f}wf​. Show that:

tα=12sαln⁡(wf (sα−w0)w0 (sα−wf))t_{\alpha} = \frac{1}{2 s_{\alpha}}\ln\left(\frac{w_{f}\,(s_{\alpha} - w_{0})}{w_{0}\,(s_{\alpha} - w_{f})}\right)tα​=2sα​1​ln(w0​(sα​−wf​)wf​(sα​−w0​)​)

Deduce that modes with larger singular values sαs_{\alpha}sα​ are learned faster. This is a separation of timescales: the network learns features in decreasing order of their singular value strength.

Solution

From the logistic solution w(t)=s1+(s/w0−1)e−2stw(t) = \frac{s}{1 + (s/w_{0} - 1)e^{-2st}}w(t)=1+(s/w0​−1)e−2sts​, we invert to find ttt as a function of www. The derivation is equivalent to integrating w˙=2w(s−w)\dot{w}= 2w(s-w)w˙=2w(s−w) by separation of variables:

∫w0wfdww(s−w)=2 tα\int_{w_0}^{w_f}\frac{dw}{w(s-w)}= 2\,t_{\alpha}∫w0​wf​​w(s−w)dw​=2tα​

Using partial fractions 1w(s−w)=1s ⁣(1w+1s−w)\frac{1}{w(s-w)}= \frac{1}{s}\!\left(\frac{1}{w}+ \frac{1}{s-w}\right)w(s−w)1​=s1​(w1​+s−w1​):

1sα[ln⁡w−ln⁡(sα−w)]w0wf=2 tα\frac{1}{s_{\alpha}}\Big[\ln w - \ln(s_{\alpha} - w)\Big]_{w_0}^{w_f}= 2\,t_{\alpha}sα​1​[lnw−ln(sα​−w)]w0​wf​​=2tα​1sαln⁡wf (sα−w0)w0 (sα−wf)=2 tα\frac{1}{s_{\alpha}}\ln\frac{w_{f}\,(s_{\alpha} - w_{0})}{w_{0}\,(s_{\alpha} - w_{f})}= 2\,t_{\alpha}sα​1​lnw0​(sα​−wf​)wf​(sα​−w0​)​=2tα​

Therefore:

tα=12sαln⁡(wf (sα−w0)w0 (sα−wf))\boxed{t_\alpha = \frac{1}{2s_{\alpha}}\ln\left(\frac{w_{f}\,(s_{\alpha} - w_{0})}{w_{0}\,(s_{\alpha} - w_{f})}\right)}tα​=2sα​1​ln(w0​(sα​−wf​)wf​(sα​−w0​)​)​

For a fixed ratio wf/sαw_{f}/s_{\alpha}wf​/sα​ and fixed w0w_{0}w0​, the learning time scales as tα∝1/sαt_{\alpha} \propto 1/s_{\alpha}tα​∝1/sα​: modes with larger singular values are learned faster. The network learns features in decreasing order of their strength — a strong separation of timescales.

Contrast with the lazy regime (anticipating Section 5): in the lazy regime the NTK is frozen at K0=2w0≫1K_{0} = 2w_{0} \gg 1K0​=2w0​≫1, so w˙α≈2w0(sα−wα)\dot{w}_{\alpha} \approx 2w_{0}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})w˙α​≈2w0​(sα​−wα​). All modes converge at the same exponential rate 2w02w_{0}2w0​, independent of sαs_{\alpha}sα​. The rich regime has state-dependent NTK (2wα2w_{\alpha}2wα​), creating a positive feedback loop — modes that are already large learn even faster — which amplifies the differences between sαs_{\alpha}sα​ into a hierarchy of timescales t1≪t2≪⋯≪trt_{1} \ll t_{2} \ll \cdots \ll t_{r}t1​≪t2​≪⋯≪tr​. □\square□

Exercise 4.4 (Incremental learning). Consider a teacher with rrr nonzero singular values and a small uniform initialization wα(0)=w0≪srw_{\alpha}(0) = w_{0} \ll s_{r}wα​(0)=w0​≪sr​ for all α\alphaα. Discuss:

  • What is the approximate rank of W(t)W(t)W(t) at early times?
  • How does the rank evolve at intermediate times?
  • What happens in the limit t→∞t \to \inftyt→∞?

What does this tell us about the sequence of critical points visited by the gradient flow?

Solution

With uniform initialization wα(0)=w0w_{\alpha}(0) = w_{0}wα​(0)=w0​ for all α\alphaα, the sigmoid solution shows that mode α\alphaα remains near w0w_{0}w0​ until time t≈12sαln⁡(sα/w0)t \approx \frac{1}{2s_{\alpha}}\ln(s_{\alpha}/w_{0})t≈2sα​1​ln(sα​/w0​), then transitions rapidly to wα≈sαw_{\alpha} \approx s_{\alpha}wα​≈sα​.

Early times (t∼12s1ln⁡(s1/w0)t \sim \frac{1}{2s_{1}}\ln(s_{1}/w_{0})t∼2s1​1​ln(s1​/w0​)): Only mode 1 has grown significantly. The student is approximately W(t)≈w1(t) u1v1⊤W(t) \approx w_{1}(t)\,u_{1} v_{1}^{\top}W(t)≈w1​(t)u1​v1⊤​, which is rank 1.

Intermediate times: As ttt increases, w2w_{2}w2​ switches on, then w3w_{3}w3​, etc. The student is approximately W(t)≈∑α=1k(t)wα(t) uαvα⊤W(t) \approx \sum_{\alpha=1}^{k(t)}w_{\alpha}(t)\,u_{\alpha} v_{\alpha}^{\top}W(t)≈∑α=1k(t)​wα​(t)uα​vα⊤​ where k(t)k(t)k(t) increases stepwise. The rank increases incrementally.

Long times (t→∞t \to \inftyt→∞): All modes converge, wα→sαw_{\alpha} \to s_{\alpha}wα​→sα​, and W→MW \to MW→M.

This is an implicit bias toward low-rank (simple) solutions: at any finite time, the network represents the best rank-kkk approximation to the teacher. The gradient flow effectively performs a greedy SVD.

Connection to the saddle structure (Exercise 2.3): The saddle points PSMP_{S} MPS​M with ∣S∣=k|S| = k∣S∣=k are exactly the best rank-kkk approximations to MMM, with loss 12∑α>ksα2\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha > k}s_{\alpha}^{2}21​∑α>k​sα2​. The gradient flow trajectory passes near these saddles as it incrementally recruits modes. The plateaus in the loss curve correspond to time spent near saddle points (only kkk modes active), and the sharp transitions correspond to escaping along the unstable direction that activates the next mode. □\square□

5. Lazy regime

We now show that large initialization freezes the NTK and eliminates the timescale separation found in Section 4. For clarity, we work with the diagonal scalar model from Exercise 2.1, so each mode α\alphaα is independent. This avoids matrix algebra and isolates the essential mechanism.

Setup. Consider a single mode: a depth-2 diagonal DLN with scalar weights a,ba, ba,b learning a target s>0s > 0s>0. From Section 3 and 4, the balanced gradient flow for w=abw = abw=ab is:

w˙=2w(s−w)\dot{w}= 2w(s - w)w˙=2w(s−w)

The factor 2w2w2w is the (scalar) NTK — it is state-dependent: the effective learning rate depends on the current value of www.

Exercise 5.1 (Linearizing the NTK). Now initialize at a large value w0≫s>0w_{0} \gg s > 0w0​≫s>0. Assume that in the early phase of training, while www has not changed much from w0w_{0}w0​, the ODE becomes approximately:

w˙≈2w0(s−w)\dot{w}\approx 2w_{0}(s - w)w˙≈2w0​(s−w)
Solution

Starting from the same ODE w˙=2w(s−w)\dot{w}= 2w(s - w)w˙=2w(s−w), with w0≫s>0w_{0} \gg s > 0w0​≫s>0, the weight www needs to decrease from w0w_{0}w0​ to sss. As long as www has not changed much from w0w_{0}w0​, we can write w=w0+δww = w_{0} + \delta ww=w0​+δw with ∣δw∣≪w0|\delta w| \ll w_{0}∣δw∣≪w0​, so:

2w=2(w0+δw)≈2w02w = 2(w_{0} + \delta w) \approx 2w_{0}2w=2(w0​+δw)≈2w0​

The ODE becomes:

w˙≈2w0(s−w)□\dot{w}\approx 2w_{0}(s - w) \qquad \squarew˙≈2w0​(s−w)□

This is a linear ODE — the NTK factor 2w2w2w has been frozen at its initial value 2w02w_{0}2w0​. Note that only the NTK prefactor is linearized; the residual (s−w)(s - w)(s−w) is kept exact since it drives learning.

Exercise 5.2 (Frozen-NTK solution). Solve the linearized ODE from Exercise 5.1. Show that:

w(t)=s+(w0−s) e−2w0tw(t) = s + (w_{0} - s)\,e^{-2w_0 t}w(t)=s+(w0​−s)e−2w0​t

What is the learning timescale?

Solution

The linearized ODE w˙=2w0(s−w)\dot{w}= 2w_{0}(s - w)w˙=2w0​(s−w) is first-order linear. Set w~:=w−s\tilde{w}:= w - sw~:=w−s, then w~˙=−2w0 w~\dot{\tilde{w}}= -2w_{0}\,\tilde{w}w~˙=−2w0​w~, with solution w~(t)=(w0−s) e−2w0t\tilde{w}(t) = (w_{0} - s)\,e^{-2w_0 t}w~(t)=(w0​−s)e−2w0​t. Therefore:

w(t)=s+(w0−s) e−2w0t\boxed{w(t) = s + (w_0 - s)\,e^{-2w_0 t}}w(t)=s+(w0​−s)e−2w0​t​

This is exponential convergence to sss (contrast with the sigmoid of Section 4). The learning timescale is:

tlazy∼12w0t_{\text{lazy}}\sim \frac{1}{2w_{0}}tlazy​∼2w0​1​

It depends on the initialization scale w0w_{0}w0​ but not on the target sss. This is the defining feature of the lazy regime: the learning speed is set by the NTK at initialization, not by the structure of the task.

Self-consistency: During the learning phase (t≲1/(2w0)t \lesssim 1/(2w_{0})t≲1/(2w0​)), the displacement is ∣w(t)−w0∣≤∣s−w0∣≈w0|w(t) - w_{0}| \leq |s - w_{0}| \approx w_{0}∣w(t)−w0​∣≤∣s−w0​∣≈w0​ (since w0≫sw_{0} \gg sw0​≫s). The relative change in the NTK is Δ(2w)/(2w0)=(w0−s)/w0=1−s/w0≈1\Delta(2w)/(2w_{0}) = (w_{0} - s)/w_{0} = 1 - s/w_{0} \approx 1Δ(2w)/(2w0​)=(w0​−s)/w0​=1−s/w0​≈1, so the NTK does change significantly in absolute terms. However, the key point is that the dynamics remain well approximated by the linear ODE because the convergence rate is dominated by 2w02w_{0}2w0​, which is large and approximately constant throughout training. In the rich regime, by contrast, the NTK changes from 2w0≈02w_{0} \approx 02w0​≈0 to 2s2s2s — a change of order s/w0→∞s/w_{0} \to \inftys/w0​→∞ relative to the initial value — making the linearization completely invalid. □\square□

Exercise 5.3 (No timescale separation). Now restore the mode index α\alphaα. In the lazy regime, each mode satisfies w˙α≈2w0(sα−wα)\dot{w}_{\alpha} \approx 2w_{0}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})w˙α​≈2w0​(sα​−wα​) with the same rate 2w02w_{0}2w0​ for all α\alphaα. Compare the lazy learning time tαlazyt_{\alpha}^{\text{lazy}}tαlazy​ with the rich-regime timescale from Exercise 4.3: tαrich∝1/sαt_{\alpha}^{\text{rich}}\propto 1/s_{\alpha}tαrich​∝1/sα​.

Discuss the difference in rank bias between the lazy and rich regimes.

Solution

Restoring the mode index, each mode satisfies w˙α≈2w0(sα−wα)\dot{w}_{\alpha} \approx 2w_{0}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})w˙α​≈2w0​(sα​−wα​) with solution:

wα(t)=sα+(w0−sα) e−2w0tw_{\alpha}(t) = s_{\alpha} + (w_{0} - s_{\alpha})\,e^{-2w_0 t}wα​(t)=sα​+(w0​−sα​)e−2w0​t

All modes converge at the same exponential rate 2w02w_{0}2w0​, regardless of sαs_{\alpha}sα​. The time for mode α\alphaα to go from w0w_{0}w0​ to within (1−ϵ)(1-\epsilon)(1−ϵ) of sαs_{\alpha}sα​ is:

tαlazy=12w0ln⁡ ⁣(w0−sαϵ (w0−sα))=12w0ln⁡1ϵt_{\alpha}^{\text{lazy}}= \frac{1}{2w_{0}}\ln\!\left(\frac{w_{0} - s_{\alpha}}{\epsilon\,(w_{0} - s_{\alpha})}\right) = \frac{1}{2w_{0}}\ln\frac{1}{\epsilon}tαlazy​=2w0​1​ln(ϵ(w0​−sα​)w0​−sα​​)=2w0​1​lnϵ1​

which is independent of sαs_{\alpha}sα​. All modes reach their targets simultaneously.

Contrast with the rich regime:

Rich regimeLazy regime
NTKState-dependent: 2wα2w_{\alpha}2wα​Frozen: 2w02w_{0}2w0​
Learning time for mode α\alphaαtα∝1/sαt_{\alpha}\propto 1/s_{\alpha}tα​∝1/sα​tα≈constt_{\alpha}\approx \text{const}tα​≈const
Timescale separationStrong: t1≪t2≪⋯t_{1}\ll t_{2}\ll \cdotst1​≪t2​≪⋯None
Intermediate solutionsLow-rank (incremental)Full-rank from the start
Implicit rank biasYes (low-rank → high-rank)No

In the lazy regime, all components of MMM are learned simultaneously: signal and noise alike. The network converges directly to the full OLS solution without passing through low-rank intermediates. There is no mechanism to separate signal from noise based on singular value structure. With early stopping, the rich regime recovers a low-rank signal while ignoring noise; the lazy regime cannot. □\square□

6. Mixed dynamics: unifying lazy and rich

In practice, networks are neither purely lazy nor purely rich. Tu, Aranguri & Jacot (2024) provide a unified description. We develop the key ideas using the diagonal scalar model.

Exercise 6.1 (The interpolating ODE). In Section 4 and 5, we studied the same ODE w˙α=2wα(sα−wα)\dot{w}_{\alpha} = 2w_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})w˙α​=2wα​(sα​−wα​) in two limits: small w0w_{0}w0​ (rich) and large w0w_{0}w0​ (lazy). A more general model for a depth-2 DLN with balanced initialization at scale σ\sigmaσ and width nnn replaces the scalar NTK 2wα2w_{\alpha}2wα​ by:

w˙α=2wα2+τ2  (sα−wα)\dot{w}_{\alpha} = 2\sqrt{w_{\alpha}^{2} + \tau^{2}}\;(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})w˙α​=2wα2​+τ2​(sα​−wα​)

where τ:=σ2n\tau := \sigma^{2} \sqrt{n}τ:=σ2n​ is a threshold parameter that depends on the initialization scale and width.

Verify that this ODE reproduces the two known regimes:

  • Rich limit (τ→0\tau \to 0τ→0): recover w˙α=2∣wα∣(sα−wα)\dot{w}_{\alpha} = 2|w_{\alpha}|(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})w˙α​=2∣wα​∣(sα​−wα​).
  • Lazy limit (τ→∞\tau \to \inftyτ→∞ with wαw_{\alpha}wα​ bounded): recover w˙α≈2τ(sα−wα)\dot{w}_{\alpha} \approx 2\tau(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})w˙α​≈2τ(sα​−wα​).
Solution

The interpolating ODE is w˙α=2wα2+τ2 (sα−wα)\dot{w}_{\alpha} = 2\sqrt{w_{\alpha}^{2} + \tau^{2}}\,(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})w˙α​=2wα2​+τ2​(sα​−wα​).

Rich limit (τ→0\tau \to 0τ→0): The square root reduces to wα2=∣wα∣\sqrt{w_{\alpha}^{2}}= |w_{\alpha}|wα2​​=∣wα​∣, giving:

w˙α=2∣wα∣(sα−wα)\dot{w}_{\alpha} = 2|w_{\alpha}|(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})w˙α​=2∣wα​∣(sα​−wα​)

For wα>0w_{\alpha} > 0wα​>0 this is 2wα(sα−wα)2w_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})2wα​(sα​−wα​), exactly the logistic ODE from Exercise 4.2. □\square□

Lazy limit (τ→∞\tau \to \inftyτ→∞, wαw_{\alpha}wα​ bounded): The square root is dominated by τ\tauτ: wα2+τ2≈τ\sqrt{w_{\alpha}^{2} + \tau^{2}}\approx \tauwα2​+τ2​≈τ, giving:

w˙α≈2τ(sα−wα)\dot{w}_{\alpha} \approx 2\tau(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})w˙α​≈2τ(sα​−wα​)

This is a linear ODE with rate 2τ2\tau2τ, independent of sαs_{\alpha}sα​ — the frozen-NTK regime of Section 5 (with τ\tauτ playing the role of w0w_{0}w0​). □\square□

Exercise 6.2 (Two-phase dynamics). At initialization, all modes start at wα(0)∼σ2≪τw_{\alpha}(0) \sim \sigma^{2} \ll \tauwα​(0)∼σ2≪τ (since n≫1\sqrt{n}\gg 1n​≫1). Observe that:

  • When ∣wα∣≪τ|w_{\alpha}| \ll \tau∣wα​∣≪τ, the effective learning rate is ≈2τ\approx 2\tau≈2τ, the same for all modes (lazy behavior).
  • When ∣wα∣≫τ|w_{\alpha}| \gg \tau∣wα​∣≫τ, the effective learning rate is ≈2∣wα∣\approx 2|w_{\alpha}|≈2∣wα​∣, which is mode-dependent (rich behavior).

Describe the resulting two-phase dynamics in words: what happens first, and what happens later?

Solution

At initialization, wα(0)∼σ2≪τ=σ2nw_{\alpha}(0) \sim \sigma^{2} \ll \tau = \sigma^{2}\sqrt{n}wα​(0)∼σ2≪τ=σ2n​ (since n≫1\sqrt{n}\gg 1n​≫1). So initially all modes satisfy ∣wα∣≪τ|w_{\alpha}| \ll \tau∣wα​∣≪τ.

Early phase (lazy): wα2+τ2≈τ\sqrt{w_{\alpha}^{2} + \tau^{2}}\approx \tauwα2​+τ2​≈τ for all α\alphaα. Every mode evolves at the same linear rate 2τ2\tau2τ:

w˙α≈2τ(sα−wα)⟹wα(t)≈sα(1−e−2τt)\dot{w}_{\alpha} \approx 2\tau(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha}) \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad w_{\alpha}(t) \approx s_{\alpha}(1 - e^{-2\tau t})w˙α​≈2τ(sα​−wα​)⟹wα​(t)≈sα​(1−e−2τt)

(assuming wα(0)≈0w_{\alpha}(0) \approx 0wα​(0)≈0). The dynamics are approximately linear and the NTK is approximately constant. During this phase, the network aligns with the task: each wαw_{\alpha}wα​ grows toward sαs_{\alpha}sα​ at the same rate. There is no timescale separation.

Late phase (rich): Once some wαw_{\alpha}wα​ grow past τ\tauτ, the square root transitions to wα2+τ2≈∣wα∣\sqrt{w_{\alpha}^{2} + \tau^{2}}\approx |w_{\alpha}|wα2​+τ2​≈∣wα​∣, and those modes enter the rich regime with the sigmoidal, self-accelerating dynamics w˙α≈2wα(sα−wα)\dot{w}_{\alpha} \approx 2w_{\alpha}(s_{\alpha} - w_{\alpha})w˙α​≈2wα​(sα​−wα​). The state-dependent NTK creates timescale separation, and the modes that have crossed the threshold converge rapidly to their targets.

In summary: the network starts in a lazy phase where all modes grow uniformly (alignment), then transitions to a rich phase where modes accelerate individually (incremental learning). □\square□

Exercise 6.3 (Mode-by-mode transition). Not all modes cross the threshold τ\tauτ at the same time: which modes cross it first? Explain why this means that a single network can simultaneously have some modes in the rich regime and others still in the lazy regime.

Solution

In the lazy phase, each mode grows as wα(t)≈sα(1−e−2τt)w_{\alpha}(t) \approx s_{\alpha}(1 - e^{-2\tau t})wα​(t)≈sα​(1−e−2τt). At any given time, wα(t)∝sαw_{\alpha}(t) \propto s_{\alpha}wα​(t)∝sα​: modes with larger sαs_{\alpha}sα​ are larger. Since the lazy-to-rich transition occurs when ∣wα∣∼τ|w_{\alpha}| \sim \tau∣wα​∣∼τ, the time for mode α\alphaα to cross the threshold satisfies:

sα(1−e−2τtα∗)=τ⟹tα∗=12τln⁡sαsα−τs_{\alpha}(1 - e^{-2\tau t_\alpha^*}) = \tau \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad t_{\alpha}^{*} = \frac{1}{2\tau}\ln\frac{s_{\alpha}}{s_{\alpha} - \tau}sα​(1−e−2τtα∗​)=τ⟹tα∗​=2τ1​lnsα​−τsα​​

For sα>τs_{\alpha} > \tausα​>τ, this crossing time exists and is smaller for larger sαs_{\alpha}sα​. For sα<τs_{\alpha} < \tausα​<τ, the mode never reaches the threshold and remains permanently lazy.

This means that different modes can be in different regimes simultaneously: large-sαs_{\alpha}sα​ modes have crossed into the rich regime and are converging rapidly, while small-sαs_{\alpha}sα​ modes are still in the lazy phase (or may never leave it). The network interpolates between the two regimes mode by mode.

Connection to grokking: This lazy-to-rich transition provides a mechanism for grokking. During the lazy phase, the network fits the training data via kernel regression with the initial (misaligned) NTK — it memorizes. The test loss plateaus because the frozen kernel cannot capture the task structure. Later, as modes cross the threshold into the rich regime, feature learning kicks in: the NTK rotates to align with the task, and the test loss drops — generalization is achieved. The grokking delay is controlled by the time it takes the relevant modes to cross τ\tauτ. Increasing the initialization scale σ\sigmaσ or the width nnn increases τ\tauτ, which extends the lazy phase and widens the grokking gap. This is the same mechanism identified by Kumar et al. in the grokking exercise session. □\square□

7. Stochastic implicit bias (bonus)

SGD introduces noise from mini-batching. Write the SGD update as a combination of gradient and noise term (use a LLM to check your answer). A continuous model is the Langevin SDE:

dθt=−∇L(θt) dt+η Σ(θt) dBtd\theta_{t} = -\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_{t})\,dt + \sqrt{\eta\,\Sigma(\theta_{t})}\,dB_{t}dθt​=−∇L(θt​)dt+ηΣ(θt​)​dBt​

where Σ(θ)\Sigma(\theta)Σ(θ) is the covariance of the stochastic gradient noise and η\etaη is the learning rate.

Exercise 7.1 (Boltzmann equilibrium). The probability density p(θ,t)p(\theta, t)p(θ,t) of the parameters evolves according to the Fokker–Planck equation:

∂tp=−∇⋅j,j=−∇L(θ) p(θ)−η2∇⋅(Σ(θ) p(θ))\partial_{t} p = -\nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}, \qquad \mathbf{j}= -\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta)\,p(\theta) - \frac{\eta}{2}\nabla \cdot \left(\Sigma(\theta)\,p(\theta)\right)∂t​p=−∇⋅j,j=−∇L(θ)p(θ)−2η​∇⋅(Σ(θ)p(θ))

where j\mathbf{j}j is the probability current. Assume: (i) stationarity ∂tp∗=0\partial_{t} p^{*} = 0∂t​p∗=0, (ii) thermal equilibrium j=0\mathbf{j}= 0j=0, and (iii) isotropic noise Σ=σ2I\Sigma = \sigma^{2} IΣ=σ2I. Show that the equilibrium distribution is the Boltzmann distribution:

p∗(θ)∝exp⁡(−2ησ2L(θ))p^{*}(\theta) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{2}{\eta \sigma^{2}}\mathcal{L}(\theta)\right)p∗(θ)∝exp(−ησ22​L(θ))

Hint: Setting j=0\mathbf{j}= 0j=0 with Σ=σ2I\Sigma = \sigma^{2} IΣ=σ2I gives ∇L p+ησ22∇p=0\nabla \mathcal{L}\, p + \frac{\eta\sigma^{2}}{2}\nabla p = 0∇Lp+2ησ2​∇p=0. This is a first-order ODE for ppp in terms of L\mathcal{L}L. Try the ansatz p∝e−βLp \propto e^{-\beta \mathcal{L}}p∝e−βL and solve for β\betaβ.

Solution

Setting j=0\mathbf{j}= 0j=0 (thermal equilibrium) with isotropic noise Σ=σ2I\Sigma = \sigma^{2} IΣ=σ2I:

0=−∇L(θ) p∗(θ)−ησ22∇p∗(θ)0 = -\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta)\,p^{*}(\theta) - \frac{\eta\sigma^{2}}{2}\nabla p^{*}(\theta)0=−∇L(θ)p∗(θ)−2ησ2​∇p∗(θ)

Rearranging:

∇p∗p∗=−2ησ2∇L\frac{\nabla p^{*}}{p^{*}}= -\frac{2}{\eta\sigma^{2}}\nabla\mathcal{L}p∗∇p∗​=−ησ22​∇L

The left-hand side is ∇ln⁡p∗\nabla\ln p^{*}∇lnp∗, so:

∇ln⁡p∗(θ)=−2ησ2∇L(θ)\nabla\ln p^{*}(\theta) = -\frac{2}{\eta\sigma^{2}}\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta)∇lnp∗(θ)=−ησ22​∇L(θ)

Integrating both sides:

ln⁡p∗(θ)=−2ησ2L(θ)+const\ln p^{*}(\theta) = -\frac{2}{\eta\sigma^{2}}\mathcal{L}(\theta) + \text{const}lnp∗(θ)=−ησ22​L(θ)+constp∗(θ)∝exp⁡ ⁣(−2ησ2L(θ))\boxed{p^*(\theta) \propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{2}{\eta\sigma^{2}}\mathcal{L}(\theta)\right)}p∗(θ)∝exp(−ησ22​L(θ))​

This is the Boltzmann distribution with inverse temperature β=2/(ησ2)\beta = 2/(\eta\sigma^{2})β=2/(ησ2). □\square□

Exercise 7.2 (Temperature and flatness). The ratio 2ησ2\frac{2}{\eta \sigma^{2}}ησ22​ plays the role of an inverse temperature β\betaβ. Interpret what happens to the equilibrium distribution when:

  • η\etaη is very small (low temperature)
  • η\etaη is very large (high temperature)

Which regime favors flatter minima, and why might this be beneficial for generalization?

Solution

The effective temperature is T=ησ2/2T = \eta\sigma^{2}/2T=ησ2/2.

Small η\etaη (low temperature, β→∞\beta \to \inftyβ→∞): The distribution concentrates sharply on the global minima of L\mathcal{L}L. SGD converges to the lowest-loss minimizer without exploring.

Large η\etaη (high temperature, β→0\beta \to 0β→0): The distribution becomes nearly uniform over parameter space. SGD explores broadly and does not settle into any particular minimum.

Flat vs. sharp minima: At moderate temperature, the Boltzmann distribution assigns more probability mass to broad basins (flat minima) than to narrow ones. This is because a flat minimum occupies a larger volume of parameter space at any given loss level — the width of the basin acts as an entropic contribution. Flat minima tend to generalize better because small perturbations to the parameters (or slight distribution shift in the data) do not dramatically change the loss. Thus the implicit bias of SGD noise toward flat minima is beneficial for generalization. □\square□

Exercise 7.3 (Anisotropic noise). In practice, SGD noise is not isotropic: Σ(θ)\Sigma(\theta)Σ(θ) depends on both the loss landscape and the data. Without solving anything, explain qualitatively why anisotropic noise can introduce an implicit bias that goes beyond what the loss function L\mathcal{L}L alone would select. Specifically, why might SGD preferentially escape sharp directions of the loss while remaining stable along flat directions?

Solution

When Σ(θ)\Sigma(\theta)Σ(θ) is anisotropic, the noise strength varies by direction. The Fokker-Planck current becomes:

j=−∇L p−η2∇⋅(Σ(θ) p)\mathbf{j}= -\nabla\mathcal{L}\,p - \frac{\eta}{2}\nabla\cdot(\Sigma(\theta)\,p)j=−∇Lp−2η​∇⋅(Σ(θ)p)

The second term introduces an Itô drift η2∇⋅Σ(θ)\frac{\eta}{2}\nabla\cdot\Sigma(\theta)2η​∇⋅Σ(θ) that depends on the spatial variation of the noise covariance. In directions where Σ\SigmaΣ has large eigenvalues (high noise), the effective diffusion is strong and the system escapes easily from sharp regions of the loss landscape. In directions where Σ\SigmaΣ has small eigenvalues (low noise), the system is more stable and tends to remain there.

This creates a direction-dependent regularizer: SGD preferentially pushes parameters out of sharp directions (high gradient variance → large noise eigenvalue → fast escape) while preserving parameters along flat directions (low gradient variance → small noise eigenvalue → stability). This goes beyond what the Boltzmann distribution on L\mathcal{L}L alone would predict. In general, detailed balance j=0\mathbf{j}= 0j=0 may not hold for anisotropic, state-dependent noise, leading to persistent probability currents and non-equilibrium steady states that further modify the implicit bias. □\square□

Learn more

The readings are roughly ordered in a way that makes sense for learning. This is a curated list of what I find important, and it is not exhaustive.

Key readings

  • The loss landscape of deep linear neural networks: a second-order analysis Achour et al. — First-order and second-order classification of critical points in DLN loss landscapes. Classifies strict and non-strict saddles.
  • Saxe et al. A mathematical theory of semantic development in deep neural networks — Read the supplementary materials section to understand the exact solution of gradient flow dynamics in deep linear networks
  • Geometry of fibers of the multiplication map of deep linear neural networks Simon Pepin Lehalleur et al. — Stratifies global minima into orbits using quiver representation theory
  • The geometry of the deep linear network Govind Menon — Beautiful mathematical treatment of gradient flow in DLNs and a surprising mathematical result relating gradient flow and free-energy minimization. Makes implicit regularization explicit (under balanced assumptions)
  • Emergent Misalignment is Easy, Narrow Misalignment is Hard — When fine-tuned on data with harmful inputs, the model generalize in harmful ways on other unrelated datasets.
  • Emergent Misalignment is Easy, Narrow Misalignment is Hard — By regularizing, we can mitigate emergent misalignment
  • Literature Review: There Will Be a Scientific Theory of Deep Learning
  • Self-Stabilization: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability
  • Beyond Implicit Bias: The Insignificance of SGD Noise in Online Learning

Loss landscape geometry

  • Deep Learning without Poor Local Minima, Kenji Kawaguchi — For non-bottlenecked DLNs, all local minima are global
  • The loss landscape of deep linear neural networks: a second-order analysis Achour et al. — First-order and second-order classification of critical points in DLN loss landscapes. Classifies strict and non-strict saddles.
  • Pure and Spurious Critical Points: a Geometric Study of Linear Networks Matthew Trager et al. — Defines spurious minima and counts the number of connected components of the global minima
  • Geometry of fibers of the multiplication map of deep linear neural networks Simon Pepin Lehalleur et al. — Stratifies global minima into orbits using quiver representation theory
  • The Loss Surfaces of Multilayer Networks Anna Choromanska et al — No-local-minima results in non-linear multilayer networks under some strong assumptions (spin glass models)
  • Loss Surfaces, Mode Connectivity, and Fast Ensembling of DNNs, Timur Garipov et al — Study the connectedness of global minima of loss landscapes (mode connectivity)
  • The Multilinear Structure of ReLU Networks, Thomas Laurent, James von Brecht — Show that local minima are typically singular
  • Classic result: Neural networks and principal component analysis: Learning from examples without local minima Pierre Baldi et al. — Original result that linear network landscapes have no spurious local minima (single hidden layer case)
  • Good review of key DLNs results: Gradient Flow Equations for Deep Linear Neural Networks: A Survey from a Network Perspective, Joel Wendin, Claudio Altafini — Also covers gradient flow

Implicit biases of gradient flow

  • Saxe et al. A mathematical theory of semantic development in deep neural networks — Read the supplementary materials section to understand the exact solution of gradient flow dynamics in deep linear networks
  • Saddle-to-Saddle Dynamics in Deep Linear Networks: Small Initialization Training, Symmetry, and Sparsity Arthur Jacot et al. — Studies the saddle-to-saddle dynamics in DLNs. Introduces the different regimes (lazy and rich)
  • The geometry of the deep linear network Govind Menon — Beautiful mathematical treatment of gradient flow in DLNs and a surprising mathematical result relating gradient flow and free-energy minimization. Makes implicit regularization explicit (under balanced assumptions)
  • Saddle-to-Saddle Dynamics Explains A Simplicity Bias Across Neural Network Architectures Saxe et al. — Simplicity bias of gradient flow from DLNs extends to non-linear and transformer architectures under small initialization
  • Abide by the Law and Follow the Flow: Conservation Laws for Gradient Flows — Gives a recipe to exhaustively derive conservation laws through gradient flow
  • SGD learning on neural networks: leap complexity and saddle-to-saddle dynamics — SGD builds up complex solutions by first learning simpler solutions and then composing them
  • Mixed Dynamics In Linear Networks: Unifying the Lazy and Active Regimes — Unifies lazy and rich in 2-layer DLNs and gives conditions for the transition between them
  • Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks Arthur Jacot, Franck Gabriel, Clément Hongler — NTK paper that describes gradient flow in function space
  • The Neural Race Reduction: Dynamics of Abstraction in Gated Networks Saxe et al. — Implicit biases toward shared representation in non-linear networks as modelled by gated DLNs
  • Alternating Gradient Flows: A Theory of Feature Learning in Two-layer Neural Networks Daniel Kunin et al. — A theory of feature learning as a two-step process between dormant and active neurons
  • From Lazy to Rich: Exact Learning Dynamics in Deep Linear Networks — Studies the transition between lazy and rich regimes in DLNs with balancedness parameters
  • Implicit Regularization in Matrix Factorization — Gradient descent on matrix factorization converges to the minimum nuclear norm
  • Gradient Descent Maximizes the Margin of Homogeneous Neural Networks — Implicit bias toward max-margin in classification
  • A Convergence Analysis of Gradient Descent for Deep Linear Neural Networks Sanjeev Arora et al. — Convergence analysis of SGD

Learning rate (discrete GD)

  • Self-Stabilization: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability — Shows that curvature stabilizes around the inverse of the learning rate.
  • Understanding Optimization in Deep Learning with Central Flows — GD with a discrete learning rate is equivalent to gradient flow on an effective loss
  • Understanding Warmup-Stable-Decay Learning Rates: A River Valley Loss Landscape Perspective — Pretraining exhibits a river valley loss landscape and gives intuition about the learning-rate schedule (warm-up, stable, decay)
  • Optimization on multifractal loss landscapes explains a diverse range of geometrical and dynamical properties of deep learning — Models the landscape as multifractal and analyses sub- and super-diffusive behaviour of GD

Stochasticity

  • On the implicit regularization of Langevin dynamics with projected noise — Makes explicit the implicit bias of stochasticity in deep linear networks with a Langevin model
  • Beyond Implicit Bias: The Insignificance of SGD Noise in Online Learning — Golden Path Hypothesis: in the transient regime dominated by drift (typical of pretraining), SGD is simply a noisy deformation of GD (it does not select different basins)
  • Stochastic Collapse: How Gradient Noise Attracts SGD Dynamics Towards Simpler Subnetworks — Stochasticity induces a bias toward simpler solutions in deep linear networks
  • Stochastic Training is Not Necessary for Generalization — Makes the implicit regularization of stochasticity explicit
  • Implicit Bias of SGD for Diagonal Linear Networks: a Provable Benefit of Stochasticity — Shows that stochasticity has a bias toward sparser solutions relative to GD
  • Stochastic gradient descent performs variational inference, converges to limit cycles for deep networks — SGD minimizes some free energy and can have circular currents at convergence
  • Stochastic Gradient Descent as Approximate Bayesian Inference — Classic paper on SGD locally approximating Bayesian inference, although it assumes non-degeneracies
  • A Diffusion Theory For Deep Learning Dynamics: Stochastic Gradient Descent Exponentially Favors Flat Minima — Implicit bias toward flat minima
  • Implicit Regularization or Implicit Conditioning? Exact Risk Trajectories of SGD in High Dimensions — Shows the Golden Path Hypothesis on quadratic loss in a convex setup using an interesting SDE model of SGD.
  • An Empirical Model of Large-Batch Training — Gradient noise scale can be used to decide the optimal batch size
  • Almost Bayesian: The Fractal Dynamics of Stochastic Gradient Descent — Relates SGD to Bayesian training
  • Catapults in SGD: spikes in the training loss and their impact on generalization through feature learning — Loss spikes when training with SGD impact generalization
  • The Heavy-Tail Phenomenon in SGD — SGD noise can be heavy-tailed, and this induces a different regularization

Emergence: empirical examples

  • Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets — Grokking: delayed generalization on modular addition
  • In-context Learning and Induction Heads — Induction heads form during training. They are important for in-context learning
  • Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs — Emergent misalignment: fine-tuning on insecure code can generalize to misaligned behaviour on other data
  • Emergent Misalignment is Easy, Narrow Misalignment is Hard — By regularizing, we can mitigate emergent misalignment
  • Neural Networks as Kernel Learners: The Silent Alignment Effect — While the loss is flat, student singular vectors align with teacher singular vectors, and this can be detected with the NTK
  • Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage? — Emergence is in the eye of the metric used to measure it
  • Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models — Chinchilla scaling law paper
  • Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models — Shows that novel capabilities emerge with more compute
